posts.title: Hanging Out
posts.excerpt: The importance of casual communal experience.
posts.body:
I have always longed to be carefree and I am in love with and hate everyone who is. If you too aren't one of the care free, you probably recognize this feeling. If you are of the carefree variety, this may come as a surprise, perhaps a delightful surprise. I grew up afraid of the world and my way of coping was to be extremely careful. More than anything, I was always careful about how much to reveal about myself while always feeling that I was revealing too much, that (too) much was out of my control. I think this caring developed into a mode of creativity which is centered in caring about things generally but also aesthetically. Caring what this here next to that there might become, caring why I do this or that and not this other thing and what it might start to mean to me and others. The artist cares, even if for the most mundane of things (like the way a paint moves across a surface), and even if at times their care turns into a fire that burns down entire villages. 

So how did I end up on the topic of caring when I came here to talk about Hanging Out? My interest in Hanging Out is that it seems to be a place specifically for carefree activity. And importantly, not carefree as one might be when alone which is a horse of a different color, but carefree togetherness in which the self is confronted, reflected, and refracted by the presence of others and through this there can be a free play (play!) of selves. There is never a goal in true Hanging Out, except a kind of opting out from goals. In college this is a time of not-doing, taken as a place of procrastinating from the work that has been assigned. And yet I am convinced that Hanging Out is perhaps the most important aspect of a liberal arts education, which is to say, of learning how to be the best form of oneself (in the Aristotelian or Emersonian sense) in a society. 

More on this another time...
